newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE-Clitoris 'discoverer' arouses controversy in Argentina.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Clitoris 'discoverer' arouses controversy in Argentina.

text.p: A novel about the 16th century Italian "discoverer of the clitoris" has aroused controversy and excited book sellers, clinching a record U.S. publishing contract for a first-time Argentine writer.

"The Anatomist" by 33-year-old Buenos Aires novelist Federico Andahazi tells the unlikely tale of Mateo Colon, a Renaissance scholar who really did claim to be the first to describe the clitoris scientifically.

Andahazi makes extravagant claims for this organ, whose identification rapidly propels his hero along a comic path to love, near-execution for heresy and eventual gory failure. "Mateo Colon discovered something which every man has dreamt of: the magic key which opens women's hearts, the secret which governs the mysterious whims of female love," he writes.

Some may doubt that things are as simple as that, but U.S. publisher Doubleday recently decided to pay $200,000 for "The Anatomist" in a deal the book's local publishers described as the fattest ever for publishing a first novel by an Argentine novelist in English in the United States.

In one of the few records of the historical Colon, which is the Spanish name for Columbus, a scholar cheekily compared his discovery to his namesake's discovery of America. So does Andahazi: "Mateo Colon's America is closer and infinitely smaller that than Christopher's ... but despite the insignificance of its size it provoked no less commotion."

The novel describes how Colon happens on the clitoris in his search for a way to woo Mona Sofia, the most beautiful and richest prostitute in 16th century Venice. Sloshing wildly over the top into period gore, the story is set in a fantastic Italy where morals are strangely similar to those at a sleazy 20th century nightclub.

Colon meets Mona Sofia at a party where the male guests are wearing tight-fitting codpieces laced with pearls and bells that tinkle as she enters the room in a low-cut number exposing her breasts. Colon soon sickens with unrequited love, losing interest in his study of corpses and forgetting to feed his pet crow. Little realising that the key to Mona's heart is closer than he thinks -- and easily accessible for a price -- he journeys to Greece to research old love potions.

Colon unsuccessfully experiments with several prostitutes before stumbling on the secret when called to attend an ailing rich widow. To his amazement, he discovers a revolutionary hands-on therapy that revives his patient, and he realises the door to Mona Sofia's adoration is now open.

Yet, despite this promising beginning, things do not turn out well for Colon. Although miraculously rescued from fiery death at the stake by a call to nurse a sick pope, he returns to Venice only to find Mona Sofia horribly ill with syphilis. He himself dies soon afterwards and is devoured by his crow.

Fearing the economic order would collapse as erotically liberated women chose poor-but-dexterous lovers over the clumsy rich, the Renaissance powers-that-be do not want Colon's find to become public knowledge, so they suppress it.

Amalia Lacroze de Fortabat, one of the richest woman in Argentina, was just as shocked as Andahazi's fictional Italian bishops when "The Anatomist" won first prize in a literary competition she was sponsoring last year. She refused to hand over the award, although she did grudgingly give Andahazi the advertised cash prize.
"This book does not defend Western, Christian values," Fortabat said at the time.
Andahazi, a long-haired Buenos Aires psychoanalyst, did not find the controversy funny, despite receiving gentler treatment than his fictional hero.

"Here in Argentina the history of censorship is very black and very recent," he told Reuters. "If this same episode had happened 15 years ago during the dictatorship I probably wouldn't be here talking to you."

He is also a little weary of the way critics have chosen to focus on the clitoris in "The Anatomist" to the detriment of the parody and social critique. "This clitoris thing, that's really all about a mythical discovery. I don't think it happened like that, not even vaguely like that. But it is a subject which has a lot to do with power because sex was always a big problem for the powerful," he said.
He said his book was really "a reflection about the way power takes control over philosophical and scientific discourse."

Milos Forman, director of the Oscar-winning film "Amadeus," and Argentine-Brazilian director Hector Babenco, who made "Kiss of the Spiderwoman," have both expressed interest in making a film of "The Anatomist," according to local publishers Editorial Planeta.
